test_case.input: Create a carousel with practical ways freelance designers can avoid burnout.
test_case.expected_behavior: Produce a concise, audience-specific carousel with actionable burnout prevention ideas, a hook cover, non-cover middle slides, and a dedicated CTA cover.

raw_output.title: How Freelance Designers Can Avoid Burnout

slides.title: Burning Out Is Not a Badge of Honor
slides.body: Freelance design is exciting — until it isn't. Burnout is real, it's common, and it's preventable. Here's how to protect your energy before you hit empty.

slides.title: Set Working Hours and Actually Keep Them
slides.body: Without a 9-to-5 structure, work bleeds into everything. Define your start and end times, block them on your calendar, and treat them like client meetings you can't cancel.

slides.title: Stop Saying Yes to Every Project
slides.body: Overcommitting is the fastest road to exhaustion. Before accepting new work, ask: Does this fit my capacity, my rates, and my creative interests? If not, it's okay to pass.

slides.title: Build Breaks Into Your Workflow
slides.body: Schedule short breaks between tasks and real days off every week. Resting isn't lost time — it's what keeps your creative thinking sharp and your output quality high.

slides.title: Separate Your Identity From Your Output
slides.body: Your worth is not your latest project. Bad feedback, slow months, and creative blocks don't define you. Build a life outside of design so one bad week doesn't feel like total failure.

slides.title: Raise Your Rates Before You Resent Your Clients
slides.body: Undercharging forces you to overwork just to cover the basics. Revisit your pricing regularly. Fair rates let you take on fewer projects, do better work, and actually enjoy the process.

slides.title: Save This Before Your Next Deadline Spiral
slides.body: Bookmark this carousel and come back to it when the pressure builds. Share it with a freelance friend who needs the reminder too.

test_case.input: Make a useful carousel explaining cash-flow forecasting to first-time agency owners. Avoid generic business advice.
test_case.expected_behavior: Explain cash-flow forecasting specifically for first-time agency owners with concrete guidance rather than generic business advice.

raw_output.title: Cash-Flow Forecasting for First-Time Agency Owners

slides.title: Your agency looks profitable — and you still can't make payroll.
slides.body: Revenue and cash are not the same thing. Forecasting fixes the gap before it becomes a crisis.

slides.title: Start with when money actually arrives, not when you invoice.
slides.body: A $10k project invoiced on the 1st might not clear until the 28th. Your forecast must reflect payment dates, not invoice dates.

slides.title: Map your fixed outflows first.
slides.body: Contractor retainers, software subscriptions, payroll — list every recurring cost and the exact date it hits your account each month.

slides.title: Then layer in your variable costs.
slides.body: Freelance support, ad spend, travel. These shift project to project. Flag which ones scale with revenue so you can see risk quickly.

slides.title: The 13-week rolling window is your most useful tool.
slides.body: Forget annual projections for now. A 13-week view lets you spot a cash crunch 30–60 days before it lands — when you still have options.

slides.title: Retainers smooth the forecast. Project work creates spikes.
slides.body: If most of your revenue is project-based, build a cash buffer equal to at least one month of fixed costs before taking on new hires.

slides.title: Save this and build your first 13-week forecast this week.
slides.body: Use a spreadsheet. One row per week. Columns for expected inflows, fixed outflows, and variable outflows. Update it every Monday.

test_case.input: Create a myth-busting carousel about why motivation is not enough to build consistent habits.
test_case.expected_behavior: Use a clear myth-to-truth progression about motivation and consistent habits while preserving the required slide roles.

slides.title: You Don't Have a Motivation Problem
slides.body: If you've ever fallen off a habit, you've probably blamed yourself for losing motivation. But motivation was never the right tool for the job.

slides.title: Myth #1: Motivated People Are Consistent
slides.body: Even the most disciplined people feel unmotivated regularly. Consistency isn't about feeling ready — it's about showing up when you don't.

slides.title: Myth #2: If It Matters, You'll Stay Motivated
slides.body: Caring deeply about a goal doesn't sustain daily action. Emotion fades. Structure doesn't.

slides.title: Myth #3: You Just Need a Big Enough Why
slides.body: A powerful reason helps you start. It rarely helps you continue. Habits need systems, not just meaning.

slides.title: What Actually Drives Consistency
slides.body: Routine, environment design, and low-friction triggers do more work than willpower ever will. Build the conditions, not the mood.

slides.title: The Real Formula
slides.body: Tiny habit + reliable cue + removed friction = behavior that doesn't depend on how you feel that morning.

slides.title: Save This & Redesign Your Habits
slides.body: Stop waiting to feel motivated. Start building the environment that makes motivation irrelevant. Save this post and revisit it when you feel stuck.

Minor overlap between Myths 2 and 3 and slight redundancy between Slides 5 and 6 prevent a perfect score, but overall this is a high-quality, fully on-brief carousel that is ready to publish with minor edits.

test_case.input: Build a concise carousel for experienced product managers showing how to distinguish a weak customer signal from repeatable evidence. Include practical tests, avoid buzzwords, and end with an action the reader can take this week.
test_case.expected_behavior: Address experienced product managers with practical evidence tests, avoid buzzwords, and finish with an immediate action.

raw_output.title: Weak Signal or Real Evidence? A PM's Field Test

slides.title: That customer complaint might mean nothing — or everything. Here's how to tell.
slides.body: Experienced PMs still get this wrong. One loud user, one support ticket, one Slack message from sales — and suddenly it's on the roadmap. This week, learn to separate noise from signal before it costs you a sprint.

slides.title: A signal is not evidence. Know the difference.
slides.body: A signal is a data point: one user said it, one metric dipped, one complaint landed. Evidence is a pattern: multiple unconnected sources saying the same thing, unprompted, in the same context. Don't promote a signal until it's earned that status.

slides.title: Test 1 — Did they bring it up, or did you ask?
slides.body: Prompted feedback inflates frequency. If you asked "does X frustrate you?", the answer is almost always yes. Unprompted mentions — in support logs, exit interviews, or unsolicited emails — carry far more weight. Filter your sources accordingly.

slides.title: Test 2 — Can you name three users with the same specific problem?
slides.body: Not three users who nodded along. Three users who described the same friction, in similar words, without being led there. If you can't name them and quote them, you don't have repeatable evidence yet.

slides.title: Test 3 — Does the problem survive a follow-up conversation?
slides.body: Weak signals collapse under scrutiny. Book a 15-minute follow-up with your strongest example. Ask: how often does this happen, what do you do instead, and what would you give up to fix it? Vague answers reveal a weak signal.

slides.title: The quick evidence scorecard PMs actually use.
slides.body: Before escalating any signal, score it: (1) Three or more independent sources? (2) Unprompted mentions in at least two channels? (3) Survives a follow-up question? (4) Tied to a behavior, not just an opinion? Three or more yes answers = worth investigating. Fewer = watch list only.

slides.title: Pick one open signal on your roadmap and run the scorecard on it this week.
slides.body: Choose a feature or problem that made it onto your list based on customer input. Apply the four-question scorecard. If it scores below three, move it to the watch list and write one sentence explaining why. Share the result with your team — the conversation alone is worth it.
